Subject: Dedicated capacity - autoscaling / throughput / queue sizing (Post-call recap)

Thanks for the time today, Samir — great conversation. Per our call, here’s a concise recap and proposed next steps so we can align the Dedicated capacity design with ParcelMetrics’ SLAs and integration constraints.

Call summary:
- Primary goal: replace current on-prem GPT endpoints with Redwood Dedicated to reduce tail latency and simplify ops while keeping per-token cost predictable for peak logistics loads.
- Critical SLOs: 99.9% p95 < 350ms for single-turn inference on structured output flows; batch embedding jobs acceptable up to 30s.
- Workloads discussed:
  * Real-time structured output (label extraction, address normalization) — latency sensitive, moderate token lengths (<= 256).
  * Reranking pipeline for search results — uses embeddings + lightweight reranker per candidate set (top 50).
  * Daily embedding ingestion (bulk) — high throughput, not latency sensitive.

Top technical constraints you shared:
- Peak concurrency: ~120 concurrent user inference requests during regional peak (PST).
- Average token length per request: ~48 tokens; occasional long jobs (chat sessions) up to 1024 tokens but much less frequent.
- Existing auth: API-key based internal gateways; preferences for mTLS for production-only endpoints.
- On-prem data retention / audit requirements for certain customers — must support VPC/private deployment or Dedicated with strict logging.

Recommended immediate actions (next 7–10 days):
1) Technical deep-dive w/ Aditya + Dev to map exact request mix and confirm concurrency distribution (can you share 24h qps/concurrency histogram?).
2) Share current candidate model(s) and sample queries + eval prompts (we’ll run a quick throughput / mem profile).
3) We’ll draft a Dedicated sizing proposal (GPU types, reserved pool size, burst capacity) + autoscaling/runbook.

I’ve attached a one-page MAP and the initial architecture diagram. Aditya will follow up with specific autoscale and queue guidance in a separate message with suggested parameters.

Proposed next meeting: 30-minute technical deep dive next Tue or Wed — I’ll send a calendar invite once you confirm availability.

Thanks —
Marissa

Hi Samir — quick technical follow-up with concrete recommendations based on the numbers discussed. I’ll assume peak concurrency=120 and avg token length=48 unless you share the histogram.

Short answers to your questions: 
- Recommended approach: start with a modest reserved pool sized for 60–70% of expected peak and enable autoscaling/burst to handle spikes. This balances commit costs while preserving latency SLOs. We can show cost comparisons in the sizing doc.
- Auth on Dedicated: supports API keys initially; mTLS and customer-managed KMS are supported on Private (VPC) and can be enabled for Dedicated via the enterprise add-on (we’ll include enablement steps in the runbook).
- Routing: we support request-level routing policies (by route tag, customer id, or IP) and model pinning — we’ll include sample config for pinning enterprise customers to a model/region.

Suggested initial Dedicated sizing (ballpark):
- Workload assumptions: 120 peak concurrent single-turn requests, median 48 tokens, target p95 < 350ms. Model: OpenModelX-7B optimized variant (fp16 / fused kernels).
- Baseline per-GPU concurrency for OpenModelX-7B: ~16 concurrent single-turn inferences at ~30–50ms per-token on A100-ish hardware with our optimized runtime (numbers vary by sequence length).
- Sizing math (rough):
  * Required concurrency capacity = 120 concurrent / 16 per-GPU = 7.5 -> round to 8 GPUs reserved for baseline.
  * Recommend reserved pool: 8 GPUs (commit) + 2 GPUs burst (shared) for unexpected sustained increases.
  * Autoscale policy: scale up by 2 GPUs when queue latency > 50ms for 60s; scale down after 10m of low utilization.

Queueing & concurrency controls:
- Use per-route in-flight concurrency limits to protect tail latency: set route concurrency=100 for user-facing streaming endpoints; overflow goes into a short queue (capacity 200, max wait 1.5s) with SLA-based fallback to smaller model or degraded response.
- For structured output flows where p95 matters, enable prefix KV caching and warm-up strategies for frequent prompts. This reduces effective per-request compute and smooths tail.

Batching & embeddings/rerankers:
- Embeddings ingestion: run on separate dedicated batch nodes (cheap T4/GPU) with high concurrency and large batch sizes (256–2k depending on vector library and GPU mem). We recommend scheduling nightly bulk jobs and a small on-demand pool for incremental ingests.
- Reranker strategy: hybrid approach — use embedding cosine distances to short-list top N (e.g., 250), then run a lightweight reranker model (1–2 forward passes) on the short-list. This keeps latency for rerank within 100–200ms when GPU is colocated or run on CPU-resident optimized kernel if budget constrained.

Integration notes (SDK/auth/routing):
- SDK startup (Node/Python): use the Redwood Dedicated client and configure route tags. Example snippet (Python):

  from redwood import DedicatedClient
  client = DedicatedClient(api_key="<REDACTED>", base_url="https://dedicated.us.redwood.ai")
  resp = client.generate(model="openmodelx-7b-opt", input="<prompt>", route_tags=["parcelmetrics-production"])

- Auth options: API keys, rotateable via Console; mTLS available as enterprise add-on. Example for mTLS: configure client certs in the DedicatedClient TLS context.

- Structured output / tool calling: use function-calling / structured schema outputs to constrain model responses. Recommend explicit schema validation in the app layer and post-validation fallback policies (e.g., re-run with higher temperature if validation fails).

Attachments: I attached a short autoscale runbook and a reference architecture diagram. I’ll follow up with a sizing spreadsheet once we get the actual concurrency histogram.

Action items I’ll take:
- Produce a sizing spreadsheet (GPU types, cost, latency estimates) once you share the histogram.
- Draft sample routing config and concurrency/queue settings for your prod routes.

If you want, we can run a quick perf profile on a sample of your queries (you can encrypt samples and upload to the shared drive).
